analysis.investment_thesis: Cemindia Projects has impressive ROCE of 27.6% and strong revenue growth (9,097 Cr in FY25 vs 2,892 Cr a decade ago), but construction and civil engineering is fundamentally a project-by-project, order-book-dependent business with no durable moat, wafer-thin margins, and perpetual working-capital risk. A P/B of 5.44x for such a business is far too rich for my taste.
key_strengths: ROCE of 27.6% and ROE of 21.8% are genuinely impressive, suggesting disciplined capital deployment and good returns on projects currently in hand
Revenue has grown nearly 3x in a decade with net profit turning from a loss to INR 373 Cr — meaningful operational improvement
D/E of 0.48 is manageable, and OCF was positive in all five of the last five years
key_risks: Operating margins of 7.74% offer almost no buffer — cost overruns on a few projects can wipe out annual profits entirely
Business is entirely dependent on government and quasi-government contracts; policy delays, payment cycles, and political risk can freeze revenue
Free cash flow collapsed to just INR 30 Cr in FY25 from INR 369 Cr the prior year, revealing the working-capital intensiveness of construction
red_flags: P/B of 5.44x is exceptionally stretched for a construction contractor with no proprietary technology or brand advantage
Recent name change from ITD Cementation to Cemindia Projects (Aug 2025) and ownership shift to Renew Exim DMCC adds corporate structure uncertainty
Finance costs of INR 229 Cr in FY25 and growing, against net profit of INR 373 Cr, means interest absorbs 61% of operating earnings — leverage risk is real
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Cemindia specialises in marine structures, tunnels, airports, and infrastructure — technically complex work, but not work that creates a repeatable economic moat. Every project is competitively bid, margins are thin (~7.74% operating), and the cycle repeats. The high ROCE is encouraging but reflects current project mix; it is not a structural advantage. I have no way to predict the order book three years out, which is a business I simply cannot understand well enough.

At P/B of 5.44x and P/E of 23.7x, the market is pricing in sustained high-quality growth for a business that is inherently lumpy and dependent on government capex cycles. India's infrastructure spending boom could sustain the order book, but that is a macro bet, not a business-quality bet. I prefer businesses where I can predict earnings ten years from now with high confidence — construction contracting does not qualify.
